sec.title: Background
sec.p: The discovery and therapeutic application of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have significantly improved clinical outcomes in cancer treatment. However, the response rate is still low in gastrointestinal (GI) cancers. The gut microbiome’s impact on immune modulation is a promising area for overcoming resistance to immunotherapy.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This study (NCT04130763) is an open-label, single-arm, single-center, phase I study assessing the safety and efficacy of fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from healthy donors in 10 patients with advanced GI cancer resistant to anti-programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-(L)1) treatment. 10 patients with histologically confirmed, unresectable, or metastatic GI cancers (8 gastric, 2 colorectal) who were refractory to anti-PD-(L)1 treatment were enrolled. Patients received initial FMT treatment via oral capsules (60 capsules), followed by a combination therapy phase, where maintenance FMT (10 capsules per treatment) was paired with nivolumab at 3 mg/kg every 2 weeks for six cycles. Serial biomarker assessments were conducted through both fecal and blood sampling.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: The combination of FMT and anti-PD-1 treatment was well tolerated with no serious adverse events. The objective response rate was 20% and the disease control rate was 40%. Clinical benefits were associated with colonization of donor-derived immunogenic microbes, and an activated immune status reflected by peripheral immune cell populations. Moreover, microbial signatures were identified for anti-programmed cell death protein-1 (PD-1) responsiveness and validated in an independent cohort.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This phase I study demonstrates the feasibility and safety of combining FMT with anti-PD-1 therapy in patients with ICI-refractory gastric cancer. The observed preliminary efficacy signals and identified microbial signatures generate hypotheses for future trials to investigate microbiome-based approaches to enhance immunotherapy efficacy.

sec.title: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

list-item.p: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have limited efficacy in gastrointestinal (GI) cancers, with low response rates and a high prevalence of acquired resistance. The gut microbiome is a known regulator of ICI response, a concept demonstrated in melanoma where fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from responders can overcome resistance. However, the effectiveness of this approach in GI cancers remained unknown and was recently suggested to be low in solid tumors beyond melanoma, necessitating further investigation.

This phase I safety and feasibility trial demonstrates that combining healthy-donor FMT with anti-programmed cell death protein-1 (PD-1) therapy is safe and feasible in patients with ICI-refractory microsatellite stable (MSS) gastric cancer, with preliminary efficacy signals that warrant further investigation. Response was linked to successful microbial colonization and an activated peripheral immune profile. Exploratory analyses identified microbial signatures associated with response in gastric cancer patients, providing a predictive signature for immunotherapy success.

sec.title: HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

list-item.p: This work provides a practical microbiome-based strategy to overcome ICI resistance in MSS (microsatellite stable) gastric cancers, offering hope for this patient population with limited options. The microbial signatures we identified enable a shift from empirical to rational donor selection. Ultimately, these findings pave the way for developing defined live biotherapeutic products instead of FMT, potentially transforming future clinical practice by providing standardized, off-the-shelf microbiome therapies to enhance immunotherapy.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: GLOBOCAN database1 indicates 19.3 million new cancer cases and about 9.96 million deaths from cancers worldwide in 2020. Gastrointestinal (GI) cancers, including esophageal, gastric, and colorectal cancers, accounted for nearly 19% of cancer incidence and more than 22% of mortality. Notably, Asia leads in GI cancer cases, accounting for 80%, 75% and 52% new cases of esophageal, gastric and colorectal cancer, respectively.1 Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have succeeded as a new treatment option for patients with GI cancer where commonly used anticancer treatments, such as surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy, have historically shown unsatisfactory efficacy.2 However, the response rate of ICI monotherapy is 11%−15% for GI cancers (phase III trial results),3 4 particularly lower in patients with gastric and esophageal cancer with low programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression, as well as patients with gastric and colorectal cancer with microsatellite stable status. Moreover, a high percentage of patients with cancer initially responsive to ICIs eventually develop resistance,5 substantially limiting the efficacy of ICI treatment in terms of overall survival (OS) or progression-free survival (PFS). The proportion of patients with GI cancer who respond initially but later develop ICI resistance could be as high as 42%–71%.68 This represents a large unmet medical need and highlights the urgency for novel therapeutic strategies to overcome resistance to immunotherapy.

Previous studies912 have demonstrated the association between the gut microbiome and the efficacy of ICI treatment, with evidence that microbiome from responders (R) or healthy donors may enhance the efficacy of anti-PD-1 therapy through microbe-derived small molecules such as short-chain fatty acids (SCFA), inosine, arginine and neoantigen mimicry.9 13 14 Germ-free mice given fecal transplants from immunotherapy Rs have shown improved tumor control and T-cell responses.10 Moreover, multiple research groups have demonstrated that fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from ICI-responsive patients can overcome resistance in metastatic melanoma, with an objective response rate (ORR) of 20–30%.11 12 However, the efficacy appears to vary significantly by cancer type, as evidenced by a recent study reporting an ORR of only 7.7% in a broader cohort of patients with immunotherapy-refractory solid tumors.15 Recently, safety and efficacy have been demonstrated from administration of healthy donor’s FMT in combination with ICI therapy on anti-PD-1 naïve patients with melanoma,5 achieving an ORR of 65%, underscoring the potential of this approach.

While FMT has demonstrated promising results in clinical studies for “hot tumors” with high mutational burdens that respond rapidly to ICI, such as melanoma, its role in “cold tumors”, such as GI cancers, requires further investigation. Therefore, we initiated an open-label, single-arm, single-center, phase I trial to investigate the feasibility and safety of ICI treatment combined with FMT derived from healthy donors as a combination therapy for patients with GI cancer resistant to ICI with exploratory assessment of preliminary efficacy signals and associated microbial and immune biomarkers.

sec.title: Study design and patient population
sec.p: This study (NCT04130763) is an open-label, single-arm, single-center, phase I study that included patients with advanced GI cancer who were resistant or refractory to the ICI treatment. As this was a single-arm phase I clinical study, randomized grouping was not implemented, and the study was conducted in an unblinded manner. Adult patients with histologically confirmed GI cancer, an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0–1, who consented to serial biomarker assessments via blood and fecal sampling were included in the study. Because this was a pilot study, a formal power calculation was not required. 10 patients were enrolled and treated at a single center in Beijing, China. Five healthy donors were recruited from a pool of healthy volunteers who successfully completed a stringent donor qualification process, including the completion of the screening questionnaires truthfully; completion of an in-person interview; completion of all required laboratory tests; negative results on all GI pathogen detection tests (full protocol is in online supplemental material). This study was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Beijing Cancer Hospital (2018YJZ65).

sec.title: Study treatment
sec.p: Patients received initial FMT treatment via oral capsules (per capsule: 0.7 g fecal extract). All patients did not receive bowel preparation before FMT. A total of 60 capsules were administered within the first week of the study, followed by a combination therapy phase, where maintenance FMT (10 capsules per treatment) was paired with nivolumab at 3 mg/kg every 2 weeks for six cycles (figure 1A). For those showing a positive response, the combination therapy was extended with full details described in online supplemental material. The complete donor–recipient mapping is shown in online supplemental table 8.

sec.title: Safety and efficacy evaluation
sec.p: FMT and anti-PD-1-related toxicities were evaluated using Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events V.5.0 grading scale. Immune Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors was used as the main efficacy evaluation criteria for all imaging evaluations. Per protocol, an R is defined as a patient without icPD (immune confirmed progressive disease) or clinical progression per efficacy evaluation at the first and the end of the study evaluation after 12 weeks of the anti-PD-1+FMT therapy. A partial responder (PRR) is defined as a patient who has iSD (immune stable disease) or better efficacy outcome at the first efficacy evaluation (after 6 weeks of treatment) but has icPD (immune confirmed progressive disease) or clinical progression within 4–8 weeks thereafter. This PRR classification was used solely to explore microbial dynamics associated with transient clinical benefit patterns and was not used in the calculation of primary clinical efficacy endpoints. Non-responder (NR) is defined as a patient who had icPD or iuPD (immune unconfirmed progressive disease) with clinical progression at any evaluation point.

sec.title: Biological sample collection and data generation
sec.p: Stool samples were collected at each study visit (baseline, weekly for Week 1–3, every other week for Week 4–12, end of the study, and study extension phase) for gut microbiome analysis. Peripheral blood was collected for T-cell receptor (TCR) analysis and flow cytometric analysis at the baselines (before FMT monotherapy and anti-PD-1+FMT therapy), the first clinical evaluation, and end of the study visit. Tumor tissues (in the form of pathologic slices) were also collected at the screening visit for the analysis of microsatellite instability, tumor mutational burden, and PD-L1 expression. Safety-related blood and urine samples were collected at baseline, prior to anti-PD-1+FMT dosing and at the end of the study visit.

DNA extraction of fecal samples was performed using the DNeasy PowerSoil Pro Kit (QIAGEN, Shenzhen). Metagenomics libraries were sequenced for 150 bp paired-end reads using Illumina NovaSeq 6000. To minimize batch effects, all fecal samples included in this analysis were sequenced together in a single batch on the same Illumina NovaSeq 6000 run.

RNA extraction on peripheral blood was conducted using the Tempus Blood RNA Tube and Tempus Spin RNA Isolation Kit (Thermo Fisher). The extracted RNA was reverse transcribed into complementary DNA using the SuperScript IV VILOTM Master Mix (Thermo Fisher). Target gene amplification was conducted using Oncomine TCR Beta-SR Panel and Ion AmpliSeq Library Kit Plus (Thermo Fisher). Following digestion, junction identification, library amplification, and quantification of the final library product was performed using quantitative PCR; the Ion S5 sequencing platform (Life) was used for TCR sequencing. Sequencing data was uploaded to Ion Reporter, an online platform for the data analysis. Subsequently, the alignment of TCR sequence and the comparison between the samples was performed.

Fresh peripheral blood samples were collected from patients at scheduled visits and transported to a contract research organization at 2 -8°C for flow cytometric analysis (online supplemental figure 5C). In panel 1 staining, the collected blood was activated with Leukocyte Activation Cocktail for 4 hours before being lysed and labeled with Fixable Viability Stain 450 to assess cell viability. After washing, the cells were stained with fluorescence dye-conjugated antibodies against surface markers for 15–20 min. Following fixation and permeabilization, cells were incubated with intracellular markers (Foxp3, Ki67, IFN-γ, BD Biosciences) for 15–20 min. In panel 2, the peripheral blood was lysed and stained with six antibodies against surface markers (CD3, CD4, CD8, CD56). The cells were then fixed, permeabilized, and stained with the intracellular marker CD68 (BD Biosciences). After washing, flow cytometry data was acquired using the NovoCyte 3130 instrument (ACEA Biosciences) and data analysis was performed using FlowJo software V.10.8.1.

sec.title: Gut microbiome species level analysis
sec.p: Sequenced metagenomic reads were quality controlled using fastp.16 The low-quality portion of reads was trimmed and reads longer than 50 bp were retained. Host DNA was removed using KneadData.17 Functional profiling was performed using HUMAnN V.3.018 against MetaCyC database. GutSMASH19 was applied for primary metabolic pathway prediction. Alpha diversity was calculated using Shannon index, observed, and inverse Simpson index and beta diversity was measured with Bray-Curtis distance.

Across all fecal samples, the mean number of raw reads per sample was 86,730,051, corresponding to ~26 Gb of sequencing data per sample. After Fastp filtering and removal of host contamination with KneadData, on average, >93% of reads per sample were retained for downstream microbiome profiling. For relative-abundance profiles, very low-abundance features were filtered such that taxa or pathways with relative abundance <0.01% in a given sample were set to zero to reduce spurious noise from near-zero counts.

For community-level analyses, alpha diversity indices were computed for all available longitudinal stool samples from each patient and visualized across time (figure 2A) as a descriptive readout. No formal statistical testing was applied in this exploratory panel.

sec.p: Longitudinal changes in Bray-Curtis distance between each recipient’s fecal microbiota and the corresponding donor microbiota (figure 2B) were evaluated using linear mixed-effects models, with Bray-Curtis distance as the dependent variable, time relative to FMT (eg, pre-FMT vs post-FMT or categorical time points) as a fixed effect, and patient ID included as a random intercept to account for repeated measures within individuals: distance ~time + (1|patient ID).

To reduce heterogeneity arising from different primary tumor types, microbiome association analyses (differential abundance species detection, taxa and pathway-level comparisons, and microbiome–immune correlations) were performed in the subset of patients with gastric cancer (GC) (n=8), whereas community-level diversity metrics (alpha and beta diversity) were evaluated across all 10 patients with GI cancer.

Based on clinical outcomes among their recipients, we grouped donors into two groups: DonorGroup 1 “benefit-associated donors”, including two donors whose stool was used in at least one patient with clinical benefit (Donor 4, Donor 5), and DonorGroup 2 “non-benefit donors”, indicating three donors whose stool was used only in patients without clinical benefit (Donor 1, Donor 2 and Donor 3).

sec.title: Strain level colonization analysis
sec.p: Strain-level analysis was conducted with StrainPhIAN3.18 The strain engraftment was inferred with the following rules: a strain from the donor was defined as “gain” when it presented in the recipient only after FMT treatment; when a strain from the donor was detected in the recipient after FMT treatment, and another strain within the same species existed in baseline samples, the strain was defined as “replace” (online supplemental figure 3A). A genomics-based strain analysis method20 was applied. Initially, bowtie221 was employed to map reads to a reference genome dataset, which is based on the representative assembly of the species-level genome bins (SGBs) defined by Pasolli et al.22 The taxonomic classification of these SGBs was assigned using GTDB-Tk. Second, the reads were aggregated to obtain per-position variant information for every detected species. For a particular species at a given position between two samples, the number of mutated positions was estimated. The species DNA sequence dissimilarity is defined as the number of mutated positions divided by the total number of positions under comparison.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Permutational multivariate analysis of variance was used to identify significant differences of microbiome composition from different groups (p<0.05). Differential analysis between Rs and NRs at the species level was performed using both linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe)23 (LDA >2 and p<0.05) and MaAsLin224 (adjusted p<0.3), while log-fold change (|logFold|>2) was measured when comparing donors. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test was performed to compare SCFA productivity between two bacterial groups (p<0.05). Moreover, linear mixed effect model25 in MaAsLin224 (adjusted p<0.3) was applied for group comparison in the scenario that multiple samples came from the same subject, with subject ID added as the random effect (p<0.05). For co-occurrence analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis26 27 was employed and the network was visualized by Cytoscape.28 As all samples were sequenced in a single batch, no additional batch correction was applied.
For key continuous outcomes shown in the main figures, we summarized the mean, SD, and 95% CI for each group/comparison in online supplemental table S12.

For TCR data, Pearson correlation was executed to measure the association between frequency of top 100 CDR3aa and TCR CDR3aa Shannon index (p<0.05). The error bar in the plots represented the SE of the data.

Multiomics analysis was performed with samples collected from baseline to the first evaluation. Linear mixed effect models were used to measure the linear correlation between host’s immune and clinical data with bacteria, while patient IDs were added as random effects. The coefficients calculated from the models were used as the correlation measurements and p values were adjusted by the false discovery rate(FDR) method (adjusted p<0.3).

Given the small sample size and the high dimensionality of microbiome and immune features, we used an exploratory FDR threshold of q<0.30 to define candidate associations in MaAsLin2 models and mixed-effects correlations. Therefore, results passing q<0.30 are interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than definitive discoveries. For the R-enriched-microbes (REM)/NR-enriched-microbes (NEM) species analysis (online supplemental figure 2A) and the microbiome–immune correlation models (figure 4C), model p values and FDR q values are summarized in online supplemental table S13.

For the machine learning model analysis, two 10-fold cross-validation XGBoost classifiers were generated using 63 samples in an independent external cohort for microbiome and pathway validation. The average area under the curve(AUC) of the 10 models was used to represent the performance of each classifier (online supplemental material).
All statistical analysis and plotting were performed using R V.3.6.3 and machine learning was performed using Python V.3.9.

sec.title: Study enrollment and baseline characteristics
sec.p: Between 6 January 2020 and 28 September 2022, 11 patients with GI cancers were evaluated for the study, with 10 being enrolled. Enrolled patients had histologically or cytologically confirmed unresectable or metastatic GI cancer and were refractory to anti-PD-(L)1 treatment (figure 1A). All patients were antibiotic-free for at least 6 months before and during FMT treatment. Dietary information was not systematically collected in this study.

The average age of patients was 64.5 years old, and 8 patients(80%) were male. All patients had an ECOG performance of 0 or 1. All patients were Asian with stage IV GI adenocarcinomas, including eight GC and two colon cancers. All patients were proficient mismatch repair/microsatellite stable (MSS) and one patient was positive for human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 expression. Additionally, all patients with GC were Epstein-Barr virus-negative. Patient baseline characteristics are summarized in table 1 and online supplemental table S1. Five patients had undergone multiple lines of therapy before enrollment into this study. Five donors were used for the 10 patients included in this study; more detailed information regarding the donors is provided in online supplemental table S8.

sec.title: Clinical outcome-efficacy
sec.p: The average interval from the last dose of previous ICI treatment to the first dose of anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody (nivolumab)+FMT combination therapy was 64.9 days, ensuring that observed responses were attributable to the new regimen rather than a delayed effect of previous treatments. The ORR was 20% (figure 1B,D) and the disease control rate (DCR) was 40%. Notably, all patients who responded to the combination therapy had MSS GC with low levels of PD-L1 expression. Therefore, when the analysis was restricted to patients with GC, the ORR was 25%, and DCR was 50%. Two patients (LH008 and LH010) exhibited immune partial response (iPR) associated with distinct healthy FMT donors (Donor 4 and 5, respectively). Patient LH008 achieved the best response of iPR with a PFS of 15 months. Patient LH010 sustained the iPR status for over 19 months of treatment (figure 1C). The FMT capsule administration frequency for LH010 was adjusted from every anti-PD-1 cycle to every four cycles, with ongoing monitoring for treatment efficacy and survival. Another patient (LH007) who benefited from the treatment reached iSD after five cycles but experienced disease progression after 8 weeks. These findings indicate that the anti-PD-1+FMT combination therapy has the potential to enhance the responsiveness in a subset of patients with GI cancer, who were previously unresponsive to anti-PD-(L)1 therapies.

sec.title: Clinical outcome-safety
sec.p: The combination therapy used in the current study was well tolerated without serious treatment-related adverse events (AEs) during the study. No participants were prematurely withdrawn from the study due to AEs (online supplemental tables S2–S4). The incidence of treatment-related AEs was 30% (online supplemental tables S5 and S6). During the FMT monotherapy period, only one patient (10%) experienced treatment-related AEs (nausea and vomiting, grade 1). During the combination therapy period, three patients (30%) experienced grade 1–2 treatment-related events primarily affecting the GI tract, including nausea and constipation. Overall, FMT combined with anti-PD-1 therapy was found to be safe and well tolerated in this cohort.

sec.title: Increased FMT colonization in responders
sec.p: Patients’ gut microbiome was closely monitored to capture the dynamics during FMT for both colon and GC. NRs had slightly higher alpha diversity compared with Rs and PRRs at baseline, but significance could not be assessed due to small sample size (figure 2A). After FMT treatment, there was an increase in observed species across groups of patients (mean: pre=120, post=136, figure 2A). This matched the results of Routy’s et al5 study, where an increase of species richness after FMT regardless of clinical outcome was observed. When the evenness of the whole bacteria community was considered, Rs showed higher increase in alpha diversity than PRRs following FMT treatment, while NRs had a decreasing trend, indicating less rare species in Rs (figure 2A).

Beta diversity suggested significant differences between patients and healthy donors at baseline (p=0.001, online supplemental figure 1A). After treatment, the gut microbiome composition of all patients was closer to their corresponding donors, with Rs showing significantly greater similarities compared with NRs (p=0.009, figure 2B).

sec.title: Specific colonized bacteria leading to a favorable response to anti-PD-1 treatment in patients with gastric cancer
sec.p: The patients regained ICI sensitivity from FMT combination therapy were patients with GC. Considering the potential difference in the mode of action between cancer types, we next focused on patients with GC to pinpoint FMT-induced microbial changes related to anti-PD-1 efficacy. Three approaches were implemented to investigate the crucial FMT-induced bacterial changes related to immunotherapy outcomes (online supplemental figure 2A).

First, by considering both the abundance and prevalence of microbes, the core microbiome29 of R and NR groups was identified, respectively. Second, samples collected at the first clinical evaluation were stratified by clinical status and differential abundance analysis was performed. Third, MaAsLin224 was applied with samples collected from Rs and NRs along the treatment, while addressing the issue of data dependence using a linear mixed effect model with patient IDs added as random effects (online supplemental material). In total, we detected 14 species enriched in Rs (REMs) and 25 enriched in NRs (NEMs) (online supplemental figure 2A).

The ratio of REMs to NEMs serves as a balance indicator30 to explore the relative distribution of these two microbial fractions. This indicator was observed higher in Rs compared with NRs throughout FMT treatment (figure 2C, online supplemental figure 2B), with notable fluctuations over time, appearing to align with clinical outcomes. Of the 14 REMs, seven species were not present at baseline, indicating the Rs might gain these species through FMT (online supplemental figure 2C). At the strain level, a total of 10 REM strains were considered as engrafted bacteria (online supplemental figure 3A). In terms of the 25 NEMs, eight strains were considered engrafted bacteria among the NRs (online supplemental figure 3A). A better colonization outcome was observed in Rs compared with NRs at the strain level represented by engrafted strain rate (engrafted strain number in the recipient/strain number in the donor) using a marker-gene-based strategy (online supplemental figure 3B). Strain sharing of REMs between donors and recipients at the bacterial genomic level was also analyzed to trace the potential source of the REMs.20 A decrease in strain dissimilarity through treatment was observed (mean of strain dissimilarity: baseline=0.009, post treatment=0.002, online supplemental figure 2C).

sec.title: Colonized bacteria formed a microbial network exerting immune-related functions
sec.p: Microbes can interact with each other for specific biological functions that further reflect clinical outcomes in patients.31 Through network analysis,26 27 we observed the REMs and NEMs showed a strong co-occurrence relationship with other members of their respective clusters, and these two clusters were clearly separated as different modules in the whole microbiome network (figure 2D). Bacteria from REMs formed a more intricate network than NEMs, with 13 REMs closely associated in module 1, whereas bacteria in NEMs are dispersed across different modules. In module 1, Bacteroides coprocola served as the super-node, the one that connected most to other group members. Veillonella atypica and Mogibacterium diversum were the super-nodes in the two NEM represented modules (module 2 and 3), respectively (figure 2D).

At the functional level, the potential capacity of SCFA production was significantly higher in the REMs predicted by GutSMASH19 (p<0.05, figure 2e). We also observed two pathways enriched in Rs (online supplemental table S7). Among them, the REM member Bacteroides stercoris was identified as the top contributor to pathway PWY-7312 D-fucofuranose biosynthesis (figure 2F).

sec.title: Donor-specific microbial traits influenced clinical efficacy of FMT
sec.p: A total of five donors were used in this study (see online supplemental table S8). To investigate donor-specific microbial characteristics associated with the clinical efficacy, the gut microbiome of the two Rs’ donors was compared with three NRs’ donors. At the community level, DonorGroup 1 had higher alpha diversity (p<0.05, figure 3A), and their gut microbiome compositions were significantly different from DonorGroup 2, mainly driven by an apparently lower ratio of Prevotella to Bacteroides (figure 3B). We further identified six REMs that had higher relative abundance in DonorGroup 1 (fold change >2, figure 3C). B. stercoris associated PWY-7312 D-fucofuranose biosynthesis was also higher in DonorGroup 1 (figure 3D). These results indicate that the enrichment of these microbes and related functions are potentially important factors in determining the clinical outcomes.

sec.title: Large gastric cancer cohort validated key taxa and pathways associated with clinical efficacy
sec.p: To assess whether the REM/NEM signatures identified in our FMT trial have biomarker value beyond this small cohort, we next analyzed an independent external dataset of patients with GI cancer13 (online supplemental material). Fecal samples with metagenomics sequencing resulting from 63 patients with GC were included for validation, including 43 long-term Rs and 20 primary resistance patients, corresponding respectively to Rs and NRs in our study (online supplemental figure 4A).

Two XGBoost classifiers were built to verify whether REMs and NEMs comprise general microbial characteristics related to immunotherapy unique to Rs in this validation cohort (online supplemental material). The model using only the REMs and NEMs (mean AUC=0.71) outperformed the model using all other bacteria (mean AUC=0.4) (figure 3E), indicating the utility of REM/NEM-derived features as baseline microbiome biomarkers of anti-PD-1 sensitivity in GC. At the functional level, the PWY-7312 D-fucofuranose biosynthetic pathway showed higher expression in long-term Rs (online supplemental figure 4B). However, because patients in the validation cohort did not receive FMT, these analyses do not themselves test or validate the therapeutic effect of transferring REM through FMT.

sec.title: Host immune profiles associated with the clinical response of FMT
sec.p: Patient immune profiles of pre-FMT and post-FMT treatment revealed higher CDR3aa diversity in Rs and PRRs compared with NRs at baseline (figure 4A). CDR3aa quantity followed a similar pattern (online supplemental figure 5A), with a strong correlation between TCR diversity and top 100 CDR3 sequence abundance (Spearman p<0.001, online supplemental figure 5B). Flow cytometry results indicated elevated CD4+ and CCR7+CD45RA− cell population in Rs, along with the lowest FoxP3+cell population. PRRs and Rs had higher Ki-67+ cell percentage than NRs at baseline (figure 4A), which persisted after combination treatment (online supplemental tables S9 and S10). Notably, Rs showed reduced CD279+cells after FMT (figure 4B).

sec.p: Correlation analysis was performed to investigate the potential relationship between immune responses and gut microbiome (figure 4C). The relative abundance of REMs and R-enriched pathways such as B. stercoris, Fusicatenibacter saccharivorans, PWY-7312 and PWY-6507 had significantly positive correlations (adjusted p value <0.3) with CCR7+CD45RA− cells and Ki-67 cells, CD4+ cells and TCR diversity. A significantly negative correlation was detected between Foxp3+ cells and the REM member Parabacteroides goldsteinii. Cloacibacillus porcorum showed significantly negative correlation with TCR diversity.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: ICIs have significantly advanced cancer treatment in recent decades, yet their effectiveness in GI cancer has been unsatisfying. For instance, the objective response rate to nivolumab in patients with GC who had undergone at least two lines of chemotherapy without prior ICI exposure was only 11.2%,4 with the median OS of 5.26 months.32 Previous studies33 have predominantly attributed the diminished efficacy of immunotherapy to ICI resistance, underscoring an urgent need for innovative therapeutic strategies to surmount this resistance and reconfigure the treatment landscape for patients with GI cancer.

The pivotal role of the gut microbiome in modulating host immunity has catalyzed investigations into its capacity to augment ICI efficacy, with pioneering studies employing FMT,5 11 12 bacterial consortia,34 35 live biotherapeutic products,36 or prebiotics.37 For the FMT applications, fecal samples from either R patients or healthy donors were applied and exciting clinical outcomes were reported in “hot” melanoma population.5 11 12 Our study extends this inquiry to the realm of patients with GI cancer who have become refractory to ICIs, a group often deemed “cold” to immunotherapy.38 The combination of FMT and anti-PD-1 therapy has demonstrated encouraging results, with an observed ORR of 20% for GI cancers, and notably, 25% for GC, suggesting particular susceptibility to this combined therapy, with no significant AEs related to FMT. The study results preliminarily confirm the safety of the therapy, and the observed preliminary efficacy signals and identified microbial characteristics (i.e.,REM) provide hypotheses for future trials and reveal opportunities for in-depth research into donor-recipient dynamics and the possibility of customized microbiome therapies. We did not employ standard polyethylene glycol-based bowel preparation or broad-spectrum antibiotics prior to FMT due to safety considerations, as our patients were those with GI cancer, some of whom had undergone GI surgery and were prone to severe antibiotic-induced GI symptoms, such as severe diarrhea. Recently reported MCGRAW trial39 investigated the combination of anti-PD-1 therapy with SER-401, an investigational oral live biotherapeutic product enriched in spore-forming and non-spore-forming Ruminococcus. The ORR in the SER-401 group was 25.0%, significantly lower than the 66.7% observed in the placebo group, possibly due to vancomycin pretreatment. The role of pretreatment in influencing the efficacy and engraftment of FMT, especially in GI cancer, remains uncertain and requires further exploration through larger-scale studies.

The elevated immunotherapy sensitivity was first attributed to the FMT engraftment. Our study revealed a significantly higher similarity of gut microbiome between Rs and their respective donors post-treatment due to successful engraftment. Similar results have also been observed in previous FMT studies,20 40 further supporting the fact that robust colonization is the first essential component in FMT success. Increased but not significant bacterial diversity after FMT was observed in our cohort in accordance with previous findings in FMT on patients with melanoma and non-small cell lung cancer.41 42 Although the gut microbiome structure from patients with GC and colorectal cancer was vastly different from healthy donors at baseline, we did observe closer distance after FMT treatment regardless of cancer type or anti-PD-1 responses. These results showed that we achieved FMT colonization in all patients with various colonization rates in the current study. Besides efficient colonization, proper microbial markers are also essential. Our results further suggest rational donor selection is an important factor for FMT success, similar to Baruch et al’s finding in melanoma.11 Among the five donors used in this study, recipient outcomes varied within donors. For example, Donor 4 was associated with three recipients who showed divergent outcomes: one patient with GC achieved iPR (LH008), one patient with GC had transient stable disease followed by progression (LH007), and one patient with colorectal cancer was an NR (LH009). This heterogeneity may reflect both the complex nature of donor-recipient interactions and potential differences in tumor type responsiveness, as all observed responses occurred exclusively in patients with GC. This underscores the preliminary nature of these observations and the need to interpret donor classification with caution. Future studies should focus on prospectively identifying donor characteristics that predict successful engraftment and clinical benefit in specific cancer types. In our study, donors whose recipients achieved clinical responses harbored microbial signatures such as higher diversity, enriched REMs and higher REM/NEM ratio, and these could be further applied for rational donor selection for patients with GC. Applying an ecology-based framework to our findings indicated parameters that may inform the development of more effective, targeted microbiome therapies in the future, and suggested how patient stratification can be used to enhance donor microbiota colonization or the displacement of recipient microbes in clinical practice.

Co-occurrence analysis of FMT recipients indicated REMs and NEMs interacted closely within each respective group, forming several functional “guilds”,31 which are microbial groups that exploit the same class of resources or work together as a coherent functional group.31 Most microbes in the “responsiveness” guild (module 1) were found to be strong SCFA producers, a physiologically important function related to host immunity.43 Several studies have shown that butyrate treatment could modulate cytotoxic CD8+ T-cell response, a major player in cancer treatment.4446 We also observed an REM member’s associated signature (B. stercoris) related to fucofuranose biosynthesis. This sugar is usually found on bacterial surface and comprises the sugar moiety of Gilvocarcin V, a topoisomerase II inhibitor.4749 Thus, the likelihood for bacterial-derived fucofuranose contribution to the improvement of PD-1 responsiveness is high and warrants further validation. Notably, we identified the enrichment of B. stercoris and fucofuranose biosynthesis pathway in donors whose recipients achieved clinical responses of the current FMT intervention as well as long-term Rs in another independent cohort, further supporting the robustness of this finding. However, this inference is based solely on pathway predictions from gene family profiles, should be regarded as associative and hypothesis-generating, not as a demonstrated mechanism. NEMs, on the other hand, clustered into multiple modules. The super node of module 2 was Mogibacterium diversum, an oral-originated microbe50 and its abundance in the tongue coating microbiome was associated with increased risk of colorectal cancer.51 An oral-originated microbe, Bifidobacterium dentium, was found in NEMs and significantly negatively associated with host’s CD4+ expression. Abnormal oral gut transmission has been reported to associate with a number of diseases, such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)52 and colon cancer.53 Increased fraction of oral microbes in the NRs’ feces indicates a more dysbiotic gut microbiome ecosystem54 despite FMT treatment, and this could also serve as a predictor for FMT efficacy. Of note, these findings on REM and NEM are currently limited to patients with GC. Based on our previous findings that different patients with GI cancer harbored different gut microbiome profiles55 and thus the expansion to other cancer types still needs further investigation. Furthermore, given the modest sample size of this single-center cohort, the REM/NEM signatures should be regarded as exploratory and hypothesis-generating rather than definitive predictive biomarkers.

Recipient immune status profiling revealed Rs exhibited a more activated immune environment compared with NRs, a trend that remained consistent even after six cycles of combination therapy. This suggests that more activated immune environment may create a favorable environment for FMT to exert its role in facilitating the antitumor effect of anti-PD-1 therapy. However, additional research is needed to uncover the underlying mechanisms. Further comparison between NR and R samples revealed a reduction of immune cells expressing PD-1 after combination treatment, which potentially suggests that combination treatment increased PD-1 receptor occupancy by anti-PD-1 antibody, re-activated exhausted T cells, and further stimulated the immune system. Meanwhile, it should be noted that PD-1 receptor occupancy was not directly measured in this study, and this remains an inferred mechanism based on clinical and immunological readouts. Significant increases of the immune cell population in the circulatory system were not observed after combination treatment in Rs, indicating that immune activation primarily occurred in the tumor, with minimal impact on the peripheral circulatory profile. Consequently, the risk of excessive immune activation and potential immune-related disorders may be reduced. However, due to the lack of tumor tissue after combination treatment, the current study was unable to compare the immune microenvironment before and after FMT. Interestingly, a separate study corroborates our speculation by discovering a similar phenomenon that the impact of immunotherapy on cells circulating in peripheral blood was relatively minor compared with the notable alterations observed.56 Moreover, by integrating the host immune status and microbial traits, the current results suggest that benefit-associated donors’ FMT has the potential to modify microbiome composition and facilitate colonization of strains with immune activation properties in the recipient, thereby facilitating the antitumor effect of anti-PD-1 therapy. However, the cross-sectional and observational nature of these analyses means that they cannot distinguish cause from effect, and they do not by themselves demonstrate a direct mechanistic link between specific microbial taxa or pathways and the observed immune changes.

The current study benchmarks the potential efficacy and excellent safety profile of FMT and highlights proper donor selection as an important tool toward clinical outcomes for patients with ICI-refractory GI cancer. Meanwhile, we acknowledge that our findings are exploratory and hypothesis-generating due to the small sample size and single-arm design without randomization. The observed associations between microbial signatures and clinical outcomes represent preliminary signals that require validation in larger, randomized, controlled studies before establishing causality. The microbial collection linked to anti-PD-1 therapy response may serve as a foundational basis for informed donor selection in future larger cohorts and holds substantial potential for the development of a rationally defined microbial consortia. Furthermore, FMT in our study should therefore be viewed as a proof-of-concept modality to modulate the microbiome in patients with refractory GC, whereas the external cohort highlights that REM taxa and microbiome-derived pathway may have broader value as predictive biomarkers and potential components of future microbial therapeutics.
